area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly and explain a stabilized normal and crosswind approach and landing from the right seat at the approach speed ±5 knots, teach the flare and the sight picture, judge when to take the controls, and spot, explain and fix the landing errors learners make most.
why: The landing phase accounts for more pilot-caused accidents than any other single phase of flight [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], and mismanaged altitude and airspeed feed approach-and-landing accidents along with loss of control and CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Every learner you solo must first be trained in normal and crosswind landings [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(d)(3)]], and a learner's first few landing attempts are where you most often have to decide how much control to take [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

prereading.what: Flaps, the five phases, the stabilized approach criteria, vision in the flare, round out, touchdown, rollout, common errors and the go-around.
prereading.label: AFH 9-1 to 9-12

prereading.what: Crab and wing-low methods, crosswind flare, touchdown and rollout, side loads, crosswind limits, turbulent air and the gust factor.
prereading.label: AFH 9-15 to 9-20

prereading.what: Faulty approaches and landings: low, high and slow finals, high and late round out, floating, ballooning, bouncing, porpoising, wheelbarrowing, drift, ground loop.
prereading.label: AFH 9-30 to 9-37

prereading.what: Energy management: what the throttle and elevator really control, total energy and distribution errors, and irreversible sink.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-17

prereading.what: How much control to give during first landings, taking the controls, distractions, see and avoid, and the instructor's practice-landing rules.
prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-13

prereading.what: Instructional risk management, and managing risk while teaching landings.
prereading.label: AIH 10-8 to 10-9

prereading.what: Wake vortex strength and movement near the ground, and the landing avoidance procedures.
prereading.label: AIM 7-4-1 to 7-4-8

warmup: Think first: your learner's last five landings were all 'arrivals': a flare started late, then a firm touchdown and a small bounce. On final the airspeed was right every time. Before you blame the flare, where would you look first: the learner's eyes, hands, or the approach? What one question could you ask on the next final that would tell you?

key_terms.def: An approach flown on a constant-angle glide path toward a chosen point on the runway, at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
The spot the airplane would hit if it kept its glide path with no flare. It looks stationary in the windshield; it is not the touchdown point, which is farther down the runway [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
The airplane's total mechanical energy and how it is split between altitude and airspeed [[24:104|AFH 4-18]].
Too much or too little total energy: altitude and airspeed are off in the same direction (higher and faster, or lower and slower) [[24:105|AFH 4-19]].
Total energy is right but split wrong: altitude and airspeed are off in opposite directions (higher and slower, or lower and faster) [[24:105|AFH 4-19]].
A slow, smooth change from the approach attitude to the landing attitude, started about 10 to 20 feet above the ground [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].
Rudder aligns the nose with the runway and bank into the wind cancels drift, so the track and longitudinal axis stay on the centerline all the way to the rollout [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
A wings-level heading into the wind that keeps the track on the centerline; the crab must be taken out with rudder just before touchdown [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Climbing during the round out because the nose was raised too fast, often because the pilot thought the airplane was sinking too fast [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
A series of nose-first contacts and leaps after a badly recovered bounce, which can grow into pilot-induced oscillations [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].
The belief that conditions are not as bad as they are and the approach is sure to end in a safe landing; one of the two sources of a delayed go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
The difference between where a tire points and where it travels. About 10 degrees makes a side load equal to half the weight on that tire [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

chunks.title: The maneuver and the standard you hold

body.p: A normal approach and landing assumes engine power, light wind or wind straight down the runway, no obstacles on final, and a firm runway long enough to stop gradually. The landing point is normally past the threshold but within the first third of the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. You teach it in five phases: base leg, final approach, round out (flare), touchdown and after-landing roll [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The POH/AFM speeds and configuration win over any handbook number [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

head: Item
Private ACS (your learner)
Flight Instructor ACS (you)
rows: Published speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots with gust factor applied (ACS PA.IV.B.S7)
Published speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, ±5 knots with gust factor applied (ACS AI.VII.B.S7)
Within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point (ACS PA.IV.B.S10)
Within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point (ACS AI.VII.B.S10)
Demonstrate and explain at the same time, and analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VII.B Skills)

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.B.S7: “Maintain manufacturer’s published approach airspeed or in its absence not more than 1.3 times the stalling speed or the minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (VSO), ±5 knots with gust factor applied.” ACS AI.VII.B.S10: “Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway center/landing path.”

body.p: The commercial ACS uses the same ±5 knots and 200 feet (ACS CA.IV.B.S7, S10), so your own numbers do not change. What changes is that you must hit them while talking. If no crosswind exists on test day, the examiner tests the crosswind elements orally (ACS AI.VII.B Note).

callout.text: Teach above the standard. The AIH calls the ACS a testing tool, not a teaching tool, and wants lesson standards to reach or exceed it before checkride prep [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. A learner held to your ±5 knots in training has margin on the private ride.

check.q: The examiner calls the 500-foot point past the threshold as your spot. What touchdown range meets your standard, and what would meet a private applicant's?
check.a: You: from that spot to 200 feet beyond it, about 500 to 700 feet past the threshold (ACS AI.VII.B.S10). Private: up to 400 feet beyond, about 500 to 900 feet (ACS PA.IV.B.S10).

chunks.title: The stabilized approach and the sight picture

body.p: A stabilized approach holds a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. On it, the aiming point does not move in the windshield, and the gap between the aiming point and the horizon stays the same. If the spot slides down away from the horizon, you will land beyond it. If it rises toward the horizon, you will land short of it [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Remind the learner that the airplane touches down past the aiming point, because the flare and float carry it farther [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

The runway shape is the second cue. On a stable path the trapezoid grows but keeps its shape. If the approach gets shallow, the runway looks shorter and wider; if it gets steep, it looks longer and narrower [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Once trimmed, the pilot should scan: aiming point, horizon, things along the runway, an area well short of it, then back, with a periodic glance at airspeed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: AFH stabilized criterion (typical piston airplane)
What it means
rows: Typically a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone, obstructions permitting [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Tracking the centerline with only minor corrections; bank normally 15 degrees or less once on final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed; with a gust factor, never below the recommended speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Landing configuration, gear down, in trim [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm; above 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Appropriate to configuration, not below the AFM minimum for approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Done before the approach, except the landing checklist [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

callout.text: Gates: go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC or 1,000 feet in IMC. In a typical GA piston pattern, go around at once if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Note the AFH airspeed window (+10/-5) is wider than your checkride window (±5).

body.p: Teaching point: the AFH says to focus on the elements that lead to a stable approach, not on their order or on meeting every single criterion [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Correct early so late corrections stay small [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. A learner who is making big changes on short final was not stable at the gate.

check.q: On final your learner says the touchdown markers are 'creeping up toward the horizon.' What does that mean, and what is the fix?
check.a: The true aiming point is closer than the chosen spot, so the airplane will land short [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Add power and raise the nose together to shallow the path [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Energy management: what the throttle and elevator really do

body.p: The AFH replaces 'pitch for airspeed, power for altitude' with an energy view. The throttle controls total energy: thrust above drag adds energy, below drag removes it. The elevator distributes that energy between altitude and airspeed. Neither one controls altitude or airspeed alone [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. That is why the AFH sums it up as pitch plus power controls energy state [[24:92|AFH 4-6]].

head: What the learner sees on final
Energy error
Primary fix
rows: Ease back on the yoke to trade speed for height [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]
Lower the nose to trade height for speed [[24:98|AFH 4-12]] [[24:105|AFH 4-19]]
Add throttle while easing aft on the yoke [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]

body.p: The trap is the very slow case. Behind the power curve, even full throttle may not add energy. Then the only way out is to lower the nose first to cut angle of attack and drag, and only then add power. Close to the ground there may not be room [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. The AFH lists unstable or slow approaches, high-drag go-arounds and steep pattern turns as places this irreversible sink happens [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

bullets: Stretching the glide with back pressure alone almost always fails: angle of attack rises, airspeed decays, and the result is a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Raising the flaps to fix an undershoot is also wrong: it can cause a sudden loss of lift and more sink [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Too high: lower the nose and reduce power, and add flaps if available [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Diving at the spot builds a sink rate that is hard to stop; 800 to 1,000 fpm is considered excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

callout.text: Same direction, use the throttle. Opposite directions, use the elevator. Both off, use both. Very slow and low: nose first, then power.

check.q: Your learner is 100 feet low on a 1-mile final but 8 knots fast. They reach for the throttle. What do you tell them?
check.a: Lower and faster is a distribution error. Ease back on the yoke and let the extra speed buy back the height; power is not the first fix [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

chunks.title: Configuration, approach speed and the gust factor

bullets: Flaps give more lift for lower speeds, more drag for a steeper path, a lower nose for a better view, and a shorter roll [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].
Up to about 15 degrees, flaps add mostly lift and the airplane tends to balloon. Past 15 degrees, drag rises sharply, and some high-wing airplanes pitch nose up [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Extend flaps in increments on downwind, base and final so the pitch and power changes stay small, and be ready to re-trim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Before-landing checks and gear extension happen on downwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]], and normally before reaching base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

head: Leg
Target
Source
rows: About 1.4 VSO; full flaps not until established on final
Manufacturer's recommended speed, or 1.3 VSO if none; re-trim as pitch and speed settle
A common practice adds one-half the gust factor: 70 knots normal plus half of 15 knots of gust gives 77 knots

body.p: Turbulent air: use a power-on approach a little above normal speed and partial flaps in gusty crosswinds, so less pitch change is needed and control is more positive. Keep enough power to hold speed and path, and close the throttle only after the mains touch; chopping it early in turbulence can drop the airplane hard [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Touch down nearly level, just enough nose-up to keep the nosewheel off first, and avoid pushing forward afterward [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

callout.text: Slow is worse than fast near the ground. A slow final makes sink rate and round-out height hard to judge, and the wing is near its critical angle of attack. Add power early; if too slow and too low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

body.p: Teaching point: learners often skip trim. The AIH notes beginners believe the yoke is enough until they need their attention for something else [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. Poor trim technique on final is on the AFH error list [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]; make 'trim after every flap change' part of your patter.

check.q: No published approach speed, VSO 55 knots, calm wind. What is the most you may fly on final, and what window does the ACS give you?
check.a: 1.3 x 55 = 71.5 knots [[24:174|AFH 9-3]], held ±5 knots: 66.5 to 76.5 knots (ACS AI.VII.B.S7).

chunks.title: Air, wind and runway: what changes the landing

body.p: Wind does not change the airspeed you land at, but it changes the groundspeed at touchdown, and that drives landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Wind also changes the gliding distance over the ground. The pilot cannot control the wind, but corrects for its effect on the descent with pitch and power [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

head: Factor
Effect
Source
rows: Same indicated airspeed, higher true airspeed, so a longer landing: about 16% longer at 5,000 feet than at sea level
About 5% faster landing speed and 10% longer landing distance
About 20% more landing distance (rule of thumb, dry or wet runway)
Each 10 feet above the 50-foot threshold height

body.p: Tailwind: a 10-knot tailwind adds about 21% to landing distance, because the airplane touches down at a higher groundspeed [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. Small-airplane POHs may not even give tailwind data; the Cessna 150/152 chart adds 10% for each 2 knots of tailwind up to 10 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]]. These effects add up and can exceed the runway [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.10]].

Landing surface/condition: an upslope shortens the landing roll and a downslope lengthens it; slope is in the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Water cuts braking, and in dynamic hydroplaning the tires ride on water with almost no braking or steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. The PHAK gives the minimum hydroplaning speed as 9 times the square root of tire pressure, and warns that landing fast raises the risk and that hydroplaning can continue well below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Snow, ice or soft ground have a significant effect on landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

callout.text: On a wet runway, pick the runway most aligned with the wind, avoid abrupt control inputs, and use aerodynamic braking to its fullest [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Teach this on the first rainy-day lesson, while it is real.

check.q: Your learner plans to land 10 knots fast 'for safety' on a 2,800-foot runway with a POH landing distance of 1,600 feet over 50 feet. About how much runway will the extra speed cost if the approach speed is 65 knots?
check.a: 10 knots on 65 is about 15% fast. Scaling the rule of thumb that 10% fast adds 20% [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]] gives roughly 30% more (application: 1,600 x 1.3 = 2,080 feet). It may still fit, but the margin is gone and the habit is wrong.

chunks.title: Choosing the runway, the path and the touchdown point

callout.text: For any flight, the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data for the airplane [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Aircraft performance and limitations: work the POH landing chart with the learner, then add the real-world penalties from the previous chunk. Know the demonstrated crosswind: certification shows control in a 90 degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO, and airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 placard the demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn in a wing-low approach, the wind is too strong for that runway; land on a better runway or at another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

Pilot capability: the RMH sample personal minimums for a single-engine pilot are a 10-knot surface wind, 5-knot gusts, a 7-knot crosswind component and a 2,500-foot shortest runway [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. At an unfamiliar airport it suggests adding at least 500 feet to runway length; under outside pressure, subtracting at least 5 knots from the wind limits [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

Available distance and approach path: an excessive approach speed can put the touchdown too far from the threshold or the rollout beyond the available landing area [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Wheel brakes stop the airplane far better than air drag, so getting onto the ground at the intended point matters [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]].

Touchdown point (S5): the AIH says choosing aiming and touchdown points must not be done mechanically. Teach the learner to choose them from the airplane, the landing being made, the conditions and the expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Wind: a strong wind on final calls for a base leg closer to the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Obstructions: on an obstacle approach a slightly steeper angle puts the touchdown closer to the obstacle and leaves more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

callout.text: Your limits count too. The AIH says the instructor must have the skill to handle strong winds when teaching in them, and must not exceed their own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:193|AIH 10-9]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: A trainer's VSO is 45 knots and today's crosswind component is 12 knots. Is that within what certification demonstrated?
check.a: No. 0.2 x 45 = 9 knots was the certification test value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Check the placard and POH, and compare with the learner's personal minimums [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].

chunks.title: Checklists, radios, the right runway and traffic

bullets: Checklists (S1): finish briefings and checklists before the approach, except the landing checklist [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Failing to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner is the first AFH common error [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. After landing, positively identify the flap and gear controls before touching either; many gear-up-on-the-ground accidents came from grabbing the wrong one [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

Radio calls (S2): at a nontowered airport, report about 10 miles out, entering downwind, downwind to base, and base to final [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. Say the airport name at the start and end of each call, use the runway number, and never 'active runway' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. Following the AIM example: 'Strawn traffic, Apache Two Two Five Zulu, entering downwind runway one seven, full stop, Strawn' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Right runway (S3): unfamiliarity, complacency or fatigue can put a pilot on the wrong surface while it looks normal. Study the airport diagram ahead of time, check runway number and alignment on every final, and go around if in doubt [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Scan the runway (S4): if traffic is on the runway, it needs time to clear; if a conflict looks possible, go around early [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

body.p: Collision hazards: most reported midair collisions happen on final or short final [[24:171|AFH 8-7]]. Most happen in daylight and good visibility, between aircraft going the same direction, at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]. Aircraft on final have the right-of-way; the lower of two landing aircraft has it but must not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. The FAA discourages VFR straight-ins; if a pilot flies one, announce 8 to 10 miles out, and remember it gives no priority over pattern traffic [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

High wings block the view above, low wings below, and the worst case is a low wing above a high wing. Bank now and then in the pattern to uncover blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Before turning final, make sure no one is already established there; a rushed, steep turn to stay ahead of someone is good reason to go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

callout.text: In the AIH study, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of midair collisions [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Make the learner call 'base clear, final clear, runway clear' aloud on every pattern, so you can hear the scan happen.

check.q: On base you hear 'Cessna on a 3-mile straight-in, runway 17.' Who has the right-of-way, and what does the straight-in pilot have to do?
check.a: The aircraft on final or at the lower altitude has it, but may not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. The straight-in pilot has no priority over pattern traffic and should have announced at 8 to 10 miles [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

chunks.title: Teaching the flare: eyes, sight picture and timing

body.p: Most flare problems are eye problems first. On short final and in the flare, the head stays straight and natural, and the focus shifts slowly from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back, while peripheral vision judges distance from each side of the runway [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. Focus too close and the reference blurs, so the pilot over-controls, rounds out high and drops in. Focus too far ahead and closeness to the ground is misjudged, so the reaction is late and the airplane can fly into the ground nose first [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].

The flare cue: hold central vision at a steady 10 to 15 degree downward angle to the runway. The point where that line meets the runway moves closer as the airplane sinks. If it moves farther away, the nose came up too fast [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. The learner can also compare the view with what the runway looked like while taxiing before takeoff [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. That comparison is a concrete sight picture you can point to on the ground.

head: Phase
What you do
What you say
rows: At about 10 to 20 feet, gradual back pressure; power normally to idle [[24:179|AFH 9-8]]
'Eyes down the runway. Start bringing the nose up, slowly.'
Match the pitch change to the rate of closure; slower if started high, faster with full flaps because the nose has farther to travel [[24:179|AFH 9-8]]
'It's settling slowly, so I'm raising the nose slowly.'
Try to keep the wheels a few inches off as long as possible; at 2 or 3 feet add back pressure to slow the settling [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]
Mains first, at or just above stall speed, in the landing attitude, axis parallel to the runway [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]
Hold back pressure for aerodynamic braking, no brake pressure at touchdown, lower the nosewheel gently as speed drops [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]
'Hold the nosewheel off; feet off the brakes.'
Landing is not complete until taxi speed or a stop clear of the runway [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]

callout.text: Once the round out starts, do not push the yoke forward. Relax or hold back pressure, and add a little throttle if needed to stop an excessive sink or a stall [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]. Teach one hand on the throttle throughout the approach and landing [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

body.p: Why it matters: touching down turned into the wind or drifting puts severe side loads on the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]. The ACS asks for no side drift and the axis aligned with the centerline (ACS AI.VII.B.S10), the same picture.

check.q: Mid-flare your learner's aim point on the runway appears to slide farther away. What happened, and what is the fix?
check.a: The nose came up too fast, so the airplane stopped descending or started climbing [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. Hold the attitude, let it settle as it slows, and add a little power if needed; do not push forward [[24:202|AFH 9-31]] [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

chunks.title: Crosswind approach and landing: crab, wing-low and rollout

body.p: Crosswind: crosswind landings are a little harder than crosswind takeoffs, mainly because the inputs must be held while speed is decreasing rather than increasing [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. There are two methods. The crab is easier on final but needs precise timing to remove it before touchdown. The wing-low method is recommended in most cases, a combination is allowed, and pilots should learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. On a long final, one option is to crab first and change to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

head: Phase
Wind correction (wing-low)
Source
rows: Rudder lines the nose up with the runway; bank into the wind just enough to stop the drift; vary bank to move left or right of centerline
More bank needs more opposite rudder; if full rudder cannot stop the turn, the wind is too strong for that runway
Controls weaken, so gradually increase rudder and aileron; keep the upwind wing down
Upwind main wheel first; the downwind main settles as speed decreases
With rudder-linked steering, relax rudder as the nosewheel touches to avoid a swerve
More and more aileron into the wind as you slow; full aileron toward the wind as you stop

body.p: Why the rollout bites: on the ground the airplane cannot drift with the air mass, the larger side area behind the main gear weathervanes it into the wind, and the relative wind swings toward the crosswind as speed drops [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]. About 10 degrees of cornering angle makes a side load equal to half the weight on the tire, and a high-wing tricycle airplane can roll over past some angle [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

Teaching it: the AIH uses this exact case. On a calm day a learner can make passable landings at the rote level, but a gusty crosswind needs real understanding of lift, drag and crosswind correction [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. So explain why the wing goes down before asking for it. And when crosswinds are scarce, don't burn a whole lesson on one drill: blocked practice looks good on the day but random practice is retained better [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

callout.text: The AFH notes that a first wing-low landing can feel like the upwind wingtip will strike the ground, and says it will not [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. Say it before the learner feels it, and show it on your own demonstration landing.

check.q: Wind from the right, wing-low method, rolling out at 20 knots. Where are the ailerons and why?
check.a: Turned right, toward the wind, increasing as speed drops and fully right as you stop: ailerons weaken while the crosswind lifts the upwind wing more [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

chunks.title: Windshear and wake turbulence on final

body.p: Windshear: a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a very small area, most hazardous near the ground. A headwind turning into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst on approach can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind that forces the airplane down short of the runway; virga with an intense rain shaft or a ring of blowing dust may be the only clue [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

bullets: Near convective weather, treat a rapid or large airspeed gain as a sign that a loss may follow, and a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].
An increasing headwind can also reduce normal slowing in the flare and lead to an overrun [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].
Be ready to go around at the first indication; some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].
Teaching link: this is where a learner's 'the speed is high, pull the power' habit can hurt. Teach that a sudden gain near a storm is a warning, not a gift.

body.p: Wake turbulence: vortices are strongest behind an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]], and short-span airplanes like trainers have the hardest time countering the roll [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3]]. Vortices form from rotation to touchdown, sink several hundred fpm, and within 100 to 200 feet of the ground drift sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. A light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution, because it can push vortices forward into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

head: Landing behind a larger aircraft
What to do
rows: Stay at or above its path; note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Note its rotation point and land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After its low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Visual approach behind a heavy, runway and jet in sight
Pick a point no less than 1,000 feet from the arrival end, with your line of sight above and in front of the jet [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]

callout.text: Landing beyond a large airplane's touchdown point moves your own touchdown point. Rework the runway math and the 200-foot target before you brief it, and remember the pilot must adjust the flight path whether or not ATC warned of wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: A business jet just landed on your runway, and the wind is a light quartering tailwind. Why is that the worst case for your touchdown zone?
check.a: A tailwind can move the jet's vortices forward into the touchdown zone, and the AIM calls the light quartering tailwind the case needing maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Land beyond its touchdown point, or wait [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: Rejected landing and go-around: a normal maneuver used for ATC requests, hazards on the runway, overtaking traffic, wind shear, wake turbulence, mechanical failure or an unstable approach [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. The AFH tells the flight instructor to stress early that any approach may end in a go-around, and that a go-around is not proof of poor skill [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. It becomes dangerous only when delayed or done badly, and delay comes from landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: Step
What to teach
Source
rows: Full or maximum allowable power, smoothly and without hesitation; carburetor heat off, if applicable
Expect the nose to rise and yaw left; hold strong forward pressure and right rudder; don't pitch up without airspeed; rough trim
Flaps up in small steps after the descent stops; gear up only after a positive rate of climb

body.p: Two hidden traps to brief: ground effect makes a very low go-around feel better than it is, and climbing out of it too early can leave the airplane unable to climb at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. And with nose-up landing trim, full power can pitch the nose up sharply toward a stall: the elevator trim stall, which must be avoided in a real go-around [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

bullets: When to call it in training: stress touching down in the first third of the runway, and going around if that is not possible, if the landing develops an oscillation, or after a significant bounce [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
For checkride purposes: go around if the approach cannot be made within the tolerances or for anything unsafe (ACS AI.VII.B.S11).
A teachable moment: the AIH example is deer crossing the runway on final, used to stress being always ready to go around [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

body.p: Land and hold short operations (LAHSO): ATC may clear you to land and hold short of a crossing runway, taxiway or point. Accept only if the PIC is sure the airplane can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance (ALD) in the Chart Supplement. Student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not take part [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Plan it before the flight: know the ALD and slope for each combination at your destination [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. A LAHSO clearance does not rule out a rejected landing; keep clear of other traffic and tell the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. LAHSO should only be issued with at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: Your learner, about to solo at a towered field, asks whether to accept LAHSO if offered. What do you say?
check.a: No. Student pilots should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Teach them to decline promptly, ideally before the clearance is issued [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin, CFIT, distraction and illusions

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: the classic is the base-to-final overshoot. An unrecognized tailwind on base makes the turn late, the pilot steepens the bank, pulls, and adds inside rudder to swing the nose around. That skidding, cross-controlled stall can roll toward inverted and start a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; at that height be reluctant to bank past 30 degrees and never skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Sixty percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

CFIT: listed causes include night, low ceilings or visibility, high density altitude and intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. In landings the usual setup is a visual illusion that makes the pilot fly a lower approach.

head: Illusion
You think you are
Untrained result
rows: Low approach; may hit objects or land short [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]
Level off high, land hard or overshoot [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]
Featureless terrain, water or snow (black hole)
Rain on the windscreen, or haze

body.p: Defenses: expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, at night or in bad weather; check the Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting; check the altimeter often; use VASI, PAPI or a glideslope when you have one [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

Distractions, task prioritization and loss of situational awareness: the first sign of overload is working harder but getting less done, then fixating on one item; stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. The instructor is a distraction too. Too much teaching on final can make you both miss radio calls and traffic; the AIH says to use only concise prompting on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]], and not to teach something at a time when attention belongs on flying [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Disorientation: rain, haze and night all push the learner low. The AIH warns that instructors may convey a lot of information while also checking that the airplane is safe, and that this can reduce attention to collision avoidance and situational awareness [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Keep the long explanation for the downwind or the ramp.

check.q: On base your learner overshoots the centerline and starts adding left rudder to tighten the turn. What do you say, and why?
check.a: 'Go around.' Inside rudder with steeper bank and back pressure sets up a skidding cross-control stall that can spin near the ground; the safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Lesson flow. On the ground, brief the five phases, the stable-approach gates, the aiming point and the flare sight picture, the go-around triggers and the control exchange. In the air, you fly the first landing while explaining it, with the learner following lightly on the controls; then let the learner talk you through one before flying it, and follow along on the controls as the learner flies [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The AIH warns against teaching landings mechanically: coach power, control and configuration changes for what is happening on that approach, not a fixed script [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

bullets: Timing: don't start landings on the first flight. The AIH's example says a learner given landings on the first flight is likely to feel inferior and frustrated, which weakens learning [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

Building blocks: master normal landings before short-field and soft-field [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. If landings stall, the AIH suggests reviewing slow flight, which builds landing skill and lets the learner succeed again [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

Practice design: during deliberate practice, keep feedback brief and explicit and avoid distractions [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Mix landing types and conditions rather than repeating one drill all session [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].
Full-stop landings help early: they build control, allow careful checklist use and leave time for detailed instruction [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
Before solo: require consistent performance of the fundamental maneuvers [[25:183|AIH 9-13]], and make the first solo landings full stops so you can stop the flight if necessary [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

body.p: When and how to take the controls. A typical test of how much control you need comes in a learner's first few landing attempts: evaluate the need for help quickly and don't hesitate to take control, but let the learner fly the whole maneuver often enough to learn it [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Guard the controls. When you need them, say calmly, 'I have the flight controls.' Anxious learners can be very strong, and there is nothing to gain by fighting them [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Never let a learner go past your own limits, and never past your ability to perceive, decide and react in time [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

head: Moment
Usually let them work it
Take it (or call the go-around)
rows: Small speed or path errors above the gate
Unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; a skidding base-to-final [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
A slightly high round out with airspeed in hand [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
A large balloon, or the nose needing to come down significantly [[24:204|AFH 9-33]] [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
A very slight bounce with no big pitch change [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
A severe bounce or a porpoise getting worse [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
A mild wing rise corrected with aileron [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]
A swerve heading toward a ground loop [[24:207|AFH 9-36]]

body.p: Debrief the landing with the learner's own description first. The AIH grading levels fit landings well: a learner who can describe and explain the landing but still needs help is not yet at 'perform,' where errors are caught and fixed without you and the outcome is never in doubt [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

check.q: Your learner's crosswind landings are getting worse after an hour of nothing else. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Blocked practice can fool both of you and beyond some point extra practice is unproductive, with rising errors [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. Break it up: mix in other tasks, or review slow flight to rebuild success [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

body.p: These come from the AFH lists of normal and crosswind landing errors [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:191|AFH 9-20]] and its faulty-landing section [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. On the checkride the examiner may fly the error as your 'learner': name it, give the likely cause, show the fix, and have them try again [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Runway looks short and wide; long low drag-in on power
Add power to hold speed while raising the nose to stop the descent, then re-intercept the path; never pitch up without power, never raise the flaps [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Runway looks long and narrow; learner dives at the spot
More flaps, less power, lower the nose to hold speed, or a forward slip; go around if sink is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Speed below target, nose high, sink hard to judge
Power early to accelerate; if slow and low, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Airplane seems to stop descending, flying level well above the runway
Hold the attitude until it starts to settle, then continue the round out; a little power if needed; go around if the nose must come down a lot [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Sudden yank near the ground; hard touchdown, maybe a bounce; or nosewheel first
Prompt power before the stall; if the nosewheel hits first and the nose bounces up, go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Long float in ground effect past the spot
Smooth, gradual pitch as it slows; go around if not down in the first third or if it drifts [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Climb during the round out after a sudden pitch-up
Slight: add power to cushion, keep the wing down in a crosswind. Excessive: go around before the stall [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Slight: power to cushion, adjust pitch, keep crosswind correction. Severe: full power, nose to climb attitude, go around [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Nose-first contacts, each leap and dive bigger
Slight: as for a bounce. Severe or growing: go around at once [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Fast touchdown on all three wheels, then forward pressure; swerving on the nosewheel
Smooth back pressure; go around if runway permits, or close the throttle and set the landing attitude [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]
Side-loading (touchdown in a drift or crab)
Airplane moving sideways or pointed off the track at contact; upwind wing rises
Wing-low method to the touchdown; if it happens, aileron toward the high wing and rudder to stop the swerve [[24:206|AFH 9-35]] [[24:207|AFH 9-36]]

body.p: Causes behind the symptoms: focusing too close makes a high round out, and too far makes a low one [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. A bounce almost always comes with too much back pressure as the learner realizes too late the attitude is wrong [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]. Porpoising can come from inattention, not knowing where the ground is, mistrim or forcing a fast airplane onto the runway [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

Side-loading is why drift matters so much. The tire tread stops the sideways motion abruptly, creating a moment that tends to tip the airplane and put all the load on one main wheel, while the wind weathervanes it toward a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

callout.text: Hard landings are not small. A 6-inch drop is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and the touchdown load can be three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. After a hard one, say so and have it checked.

check.q: Your learner floats halfway down a 3,000-foot runway in a gusty crosswind and starts to drift. What is the call?
check.a: Go around. If the landing cannot be made in the first third, or the airplane drifts, execute a go-around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-6. Runway shape during stabilized approach. (AFH 9-5)
f1.alt: Three views of runway 25 from the cockpit on a 3 degree approach: at 1,600 feet from the threshold and 105 feet altitude, at 800 feet and 52 feet, and at 400 feet and 26 feet. The runway trapezoid grows larger but keeps the same shape, and the aiming point marker stays in the same place.

f2.caption: Figure 9-9. To obtain necessary visual cues, the pilot should look toward the runway at a shallow angle. (AFH 9-8)
f2.alt: An airplane in the round out over the threshold of runway 27, with three lines of sight drawn from the pilot to the runway: a long shallow yellow line far ahead, an orange line in the middle, and a steeper yellow line closer in, with the angle marked 10 to 15 degrees.

f3.caption: Figure 4-13. Energy error management. (AFH 4-14)
f3.alt: Top: an airplane below a dashed desired glideslope to a runway. Bottom: an altitude versus airspeed chart with a magnified circle. Point A, the desired state, is at the center. Points B, C and D sit below it: B low and slow, C low on speed, D low and fast. A blue arrow marks total energy error (throttle), and a green arrow marks energy distribution error (elevator).

f4.caption: Figure 9-32. Rounding out too high. (AFH 9-31)
f4.alt: An airplane descends toward runway 34, rounds out too early and levels off well above the runway, flies level with increasing angle of attack, then drops onto the runway near the numbers.

f5.caption: Figure 9-34. Ballooning during roundout. (AFH 9-33)
f5.alt: An airplane on final over the runway 34 threshold rounds out, then its flight path curves upward and it climbs away from the runway in a nose-high attitude.

f6.caption: Figure 9-35. Bouncing during touchdown. (AFH 9-33)
f6.alt: An airplane touches down hard, the tail is forced down, the angle of attack increases rapidly, and it bounces back into the air before settling again. Labels show small angle of attack, decreasing angle of attack, rapid increase in angle of attack, and normal angle of attack.

f7.caption: Figure 9-37. Drifting during touchdown. (AFH 9-35)
f7.alt: Front view of a high-wing airplane touching down while drifting, with wind from the right. Arrows show wind force on the side, inertia force at the center of gravity, weight, and the tire's force resisting side motion, which together tend to tip the airplane and raise the upwind wing.

scenario.title: Gusty crosswind circuits before a first solo
scenario.setup: Your learner is close to solo in a fixed-gear trainer at a busy towered airport. Runway 27 is 4,500 feet and damp after a shower; runway 33 crosses it. Wind is 300 at 12 gusting 20. A regional jet is landing on 33 ahead of you. A line of rain showers is 10 miles west. The learner wants to finish today because the solo is scheduled for tomorrow morning.

questions.q: What do you check before the first circuit, beyond the POH landing chart?
questions.a: The crosswind component against the demonstrated value (0.2 VSO at certification) [[24:190|AFH 9-19]] and the learner's personal minimums, which outside pressure should tighten, not loosen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. A damp runway means possible hydroplaning [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

questions.q: What approach speed and flap setting do you brief for the gusts?
questions.a: A common practice is normal speed plus half the gust factor, here half of 8 knots, so plus 4, with partial flaps for more control in a gusty crosswind, always within POH guidance [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Your own window is ±5 knots of that target (ACS AI.VII.B.S7).

questions.q: Tower clears you to land 27. The regional jet landed on 33 and you will cross its path. What is the plan?
questions.a: Landing behind a larger aircraft on a crossing runway: cross above its flight path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Its vortices sink several hundred fpm behind it, so staying at or above its path keeps you clear [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

questions.q: Tower then offers 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 33.' Your learner reaches for the mic to accept. What do you do?
questions.a: Decide as PIC before reading back: you can decline. You are on a gusty, damp runway with a learner flying, so the ALD must clearly work. If accepted, it still allows a rejected landing [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. With a solo next day, it is also a chance to teach that a student pilot should not accept LAHSO [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: On short final the airspeed jumps 12 knots and the showers are closer. What do you teach in that moment?
questions.a: Near convective weather a sudden gain may come before a loss and is a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Go around early; some microbursts cannot be escaped [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

questions.q: The learner keeps looking at you for approval during the flare and lands with a side drift. How do you handle the next circuit?
questions.a: Use concise prompts only on final [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Fix the eyes first: steady view down the runway at a shallow angle [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. Insist on the wing-low correction held to touchdown, because drift side-loads the gear [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. If the wind is beyond the learner today, stopping is the lesson [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing and landing checklists at the right points and explain why briefings come before the approach.
skills.practice: Do the downwind flow, then the landing check on final, and say aloud why [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Make the pattern radio calls, towered or nontowered, and explain the phraseology.
skills.practice: Script the 10-mile, downwind, base and final calls with the airport name at both ends [[24:170|AFH 8-6]] [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Confirm the correct or assigned runway on final and explain how you avoid a wrong-surface landing.
skills.practice: On every final, call the runway number and alignment out loud; study the diagram before unfamiliar airports [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the runway and surrounding area for traffic and obstructions and say what you see.
skills.practice: 'Base clear, final clear, runway clear' on every circuit; bank to uncover blind spots [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

skills.do: Pick and aim for a touchdown point that fits the wind, surface and obstructions, and explain why.
skills.practice: Choose a different point each circuit and explain the choice instead of always using the same marks [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

skills.do: Set the recommended configuration, airspeed and trim, and adjust pitch and power to stay stabilized, explaining each correction in energy terms.
skills.practice: Have a friend in the right seat call out deviations; answer each with 'throttle,' 'elevator' or 'both' [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

skills.do: Maintain manufacturer’s published approach airspeed or in its absence not more than 1.3 times the stalling speed or the minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (VSO), ±5 knots with gust factor applied (ACS AI.VII.B.S7), while talking.
skills.practice: Fly finals with nonstop patter until your speed stays in the window; trim after every flap change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and the right crosswind correction from final through the rollout, and explain crab and wing-low.
skills.practice: On crosswind days, fly wing-low from 300 feet down and narrate the growing control inputs [[24:188|AFH 9-17]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Make a smooth, timely round out and touchdown while describing the sight picture.
skills.practice: Practice the patter for the steady 10 to 15 degree view and the closing intercept point [[24:178|AFH 9-7]] [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway center/landing path (ACS AI.VII.B.S10).
skills.practice: Have someone name a point on each downwind; log the miss distance from the runway markings.

skills.do: Go around without delay when the approach is outside tolerance or unsafe, flying power, attitude and configuration while explaining.
skills.practice: Plan unannounced go-arounds at different heights, including low ones in ground effect [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common landing errors, usually a simulated error the examiner flies as your 'learner.'
skills.practice: For each row of the error table, practice saying what you see, the cause and the fix in one breath [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

quiz.q: In the AFH energy model, which control changes the airplane's total energy?
quiz.why: The throttle is the total energy controller; the elevator distributes energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

quiz.q: A learner on final is high and slow. What type of energy error is that?
options: No error if the path is steep
quiz.why: Altitude and airspeed off in opposite directions is an energy distribution error [[24:105|AFH 4-19]].

quiz.q: Up to about what flap deflection do flaps produce mostly lift and a tendency to balloon?
quiz.why: Deflection up to 15 degrees produces mostly lift with little drag, with a tendency to balloon [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: What steady downward viewing angle does the AFH give for central vision as the flare starts?
quiz.why: Focus central vision at a shallow downward angle of 10 to 15 degrees relative to the runway [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].

quiz.q: Why does the round out need a faster pitch change with full flaps?
options: Full flaps raise the stall speed
The nose starts lower, so it must travel farther to the landing attitude
quiz.why: With full flaps the approach attitude is lower, and the round out starts at about the same height, so pitch must increase faster [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].

quiz.q: In a wing-low crosswind round out, what must happen to the rudder and aileron deflections as the airplane slows?
options: Hold them exactly where they were on final
Reduce them, since the wind matters less
quiz.why: As airspeed drops the controls get less effective, so rudder and aileron deflection must gradually increase to keep the drift correction [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

quiz.q: About how much cornering angle makes a tire side load equal to half the weight it carries?
quiz.why: As little as 10 degrees of cornering angle creates a side load equal to half the supported weight [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, what are the two usual sources of delay in starting a go-around?
quiz.why: Delay normally stems from landing expectancy (set) and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Where does a pilot find the Available Landing Distance (ALD) needed to decide on a LAHSO clearance?
options: Only from the tower on request
In the Chart Supplement and the Terminal Procedures Publications
quiz.why: ALD data are published in the Chart Supplement and the U.S. Terminal Procedures Publications; controllers also give it on request [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH say about coaching on final approach?
options: Take the controls on every approach
quiz.why: Excessive teaching on final can cause missed radio calls; use only concise prompting on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is low and slow on short final, well behind the power curve. Full power does not stop the sink. What does the AFH say is the only recourse?
options: Raise the nose to stretch the glide
Retract the flaps to reduce drag
Lower the nose first to cut angle of attack and drag, then add power
Hold attitude and wait for ground effect
final_quiz.why: When excess power is negative, first trade altitude for speed by pushing forward, then add throttle; near the ground there may not be room [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: Short final at an unfamiliar airport at dusk, your learner is not sure whether the lit strip ahead is the runway or a parallel taxiway. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Continue and decide in the flare
Go around and consider the situation further
Ask the learner to check the moving map and land
Land on whichever surface is longer
final_quiz.why: Verify runway alignment and number on final; if there is doubt over the landing surface, go around and consider the situation further [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner rounds out high: the airplane is level 8 feet above the runway with airspeed still in hand. What do you coach?
options: Hold the attitude until it settles, then continue the round out
Pull to the full landing attitude now
Close the throttle and let it drop
final_quiz.why: Hold pitch constant until it decelerates and starts down, then continue the round out; add a little power if needed. Pulling further stalls it and it drops hard [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

final_quiz.q: On a 1-mile final your learner is high and fast and pushes the nose over to dive at the spot. Why does the AFH object?
options: It builds a high sink rate that is hard to stop near the ground; use flaps, less power with a lower nose, or a forward slip instead
final_quiz.why: A sink rate over 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive and hard to slow before ground contact, so don't dive at the aiming point; steepen with flaps and power or a forward slip [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's touchdowns come nose first, each leap and dive bigger, while they make quick pitch and power corrections. What is the AFH call?
options: Keep correcting; it will damp out
Go around immediately: full power, directional control, nose to a safe climb attitude
Push forward to hold it on the runway
final_quiz.why: In a severe or worsening porpoise, untimely inputs make each contact worse and can collapse the nose gear; go around at once [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

final_quiz.q: A fast learner forces the airplane onto all three wheels and pushes forward. The airplane starts to swerve on the nosewheel. What is this and the usual fix?
options: Wheelbarrowing; smooth back pressure, or a go-around if runway permits
Ground loop; full brake on the high wing
final_quiz.why: Wheelbarrowing usually follows a fast simultaneous touchdown plus forward pressure; correct with back pressure, or go around if conditions permit [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flares every landing too high and drops in. In the debrief they say they watch the runway right over the nose. What is the likely cause?
options: Focusing too close, which blurs the reference and leads to over-control and a high round out
final_quiz.why: A reference too close or looking straight down blurs, and the pilot tends to over-control, round out high and make drop-in landings [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: Long final in a steady crosswind. Your learner flies the crab well but keeps landing with side drift. What does the AFH offer?
options: Crab all the way and kick it straight in the flare only
Crab first on a long final, then change smoothly to the wing-low method before the round out
Use no correction until over the runway
final_quiz.why: On a long final, one option is to crab first and transition to wing-low before the round out; removing a crab too early or late side-loads the gear [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

final_quiz.q: Nosewheel steering is linked to the rudder, and you are holding right rudder in a crosswind as the nosewheel comes down. What should the learner do?
options: Hold the rudder to keep straight
Relax the corrective rudder as the nosewheel touches
Push forward to plant the nosewheel
final_quiz.why: The nosewheel is not aligned with the runway while opposite rudder is held, so relax rudder as it touches to prevent a swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

final_quiz.q: During a go-around from a full-flap, nose-up trimmed approach, your learner applies full power and the nose rises sharply. What hazard are you watching for?
final_quiz.why: Propwash plus nose-up trim can pitch the nose sharply up toward a stall; it must be avoided in a real go-around with forward pressure and trim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You are landing behind a large airplane that is departing on the same runway. Where should you touch down?
final_quiz.why: Landing behind a departing larger aircraft, same runway: note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Night approach to a runway with bright runway and approach lights and almost no lights around it. Which way will an untrained learner err?
options: Low, because the runway looks farther away
High, because the runway looks closer than it is
final_quiz.why: Bright lighting with few surrounding lights can create the illusion of less distance, and the pilot often flies a higher approach [[23:76|IFH 3-9]] [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

final_quiz.q: A learner's touchdown is drifting left with a crab still in, and the airplane swerves after contact. What does the AFH say to do?
options: Aileron toward the high wing and rudder to stop the swerve; brakes only if rudder is not enough
Push forward to plant the nosewheel
final_quiz.why: If it touches down drifting or crabbed, apply aileron toward the high wing and stop the swerve with rudder; use brakes only when rudder is inadequate [[24:207|AFH 9-36]].

takeaways: You fly the approach speed ±5 knots and touch down within 200 feet of the point while explaining; your private learner is held to +10/-5 and 400 feet.
Stabilized means a fixed aiming point and an unchanging runway shape; go around if unstable below 300 feet AGL in the pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
Teach in energy terms: same-direction errors are throttle, opposite-direction errors are elevator, and very slow and low is nose first [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Most flare errors start with the eyes: a steady, shallow look down the runway [[24:178|AFH 9-7]].
Wing-low from final through the rollout prevents side-loading; ailerons go fully into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
A severe balloon, bounce or porpoise is a go-around, not a save.
Coach briefly on final, take the controls without hesitation when needed, and say it calmly [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
cfi_notes: If no crosswind exists on test day, the examiner tests crosswind knowledge orally (ACS AI.VII.B Note). Have the wing-low patter and the rollout aileron story ready.

Sources disagree on airspeed windows: the AFH stabilized-approach criteria allow +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], which matches the private ACS. Your CFI and commercial window is ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.B.S7). Teach the tighter number.

Sources disagree on the hydroplaning formula: the PHAK uses 9 times the square root of tire pressure [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]], the AFH uses 8.6 [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]. For 25 psi that is 45 versus 43 knots. Either way, landing fast raises the risk.

Sources differ slightly on excess speed: the PHAK says a 10% excess landing speed causes at least 21% more landing distance, then uses 20% in its summary [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]; AC 91-79B uses 20% as a rule of thumb [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]. Treat both as rough.

The gust-factor rule (add half the gust factor) is described as what pilots often use, not a rule, and the AFH says the POH speeds and flap settings govern [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. The ACS only says 'with gust factor applied,' so brief your method before the checkride.

The AFH says the wing-low method is recommended in most cases but that pilots should learn both methods [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Teach the crab on long finals and the transition to wing-low, not just one technique.

The AIH warns that teaching landings mechanically produces unstable approaches and faulty landings [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Avoid fixed power settings at fixed points as the only method; teach the learner to read the picture.
The AFH uses 'student,' the AIH uses 'learner.' Same person.
gaps: Approach speeds, flap settings, minimum approach power and the demonstrated crosswind are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No source describes how the flare sight picture differs from the right seat, or how to adjust your own references when instructing from it. Build them in practice.
No source gives a crosswind 'limit' for learners; the RMH sample of 7 knots is only an example [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. Set it with the learner and your school.
No source gives a specific escape technique for a microburst on approach in a light single; AC 00-54 (FAA Pilot Wind Shear Guide), named by the PHAK [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]], is not in the resources.
Available Landing Distance for LAHSO and airport slope are in the Chart Supplement, which is not in the resources.

activities.title: Read the energy error chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its pin on the magnified circle.

activities.title: Approach speed and landing distance math
activities.intro: Work each one from the lesson's rules, then type your answer.

items.q: No published approach speed; VSO is 48 knots. What is the highest final approach speed the ACS allows, before the ±5 knot tolerance?
POH approach speed 65 knots. Wind 280 at 12 gusting 22. Using the common half-gust-factor practice, what is your target?
items.why: Gust factor 22 - 12 = 10 knots; half is 5; 65 + 5 = 70 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

items.q: POH landing distance 1,400 feet. You must land with a 10-knot tailwind. About how much distance now?
items.why: A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21%: 1,400 x 1.21 = 1,694 feet [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]].

items.q: Same 1,400-foot POH distance, but you cross the threshold at 80 feet instead of 50. About how much extra distance?
POH landing distance 1,400 feet at the chart weight. Today you are 10% heavier. About how much landing distance?
items.why: Landing distance varies in direct proportion to weight: 10% heavier gives about 10% more, 1,400 x 1.1 = 1,540 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

activities.title: From short final to the rollout
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put your demonstration callouts in order, then tap Check.
steps: Eyes from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back
About 10 to 20 feet: start gradual back pressure, power to idle
Hold the wheels a few inches off as long as possible
Touch down on the mains in the landing attitude
Hold back pressure, feet off the brakes
Lower the nosewheel gently as speed decreases
Brakes only after the nosewheel is down and directional control is established

activities.title: Upwind or downwind side?
activities.intro: Tap each item, then tap the side of the airplane it belongs to in a wing-low crosswind landing.

items.t: The rudder pedal you press to keep the nose straight
The first main wheel to touch down
The main wheel that settles last
Where the ailerons are held as you stop
The way the nose tends to weathervane on the rollout
The wing that tends to rise after touchdown
The direction a crab heading is turned

activities.title: True or false: go-arounds and LAHSO
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH says a go-around is usually a sign of insufficient skill, so learners should avoid needing one.
cards.why: False. The AFH calls that assumption a fallacy and tells instructors to stress that any approach may end in a go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: In a go-around, raise all the flaps at once to get rid of drag as fast as possible.
cards.why: False. Retract them in small increments as the airplane accelerates; a sudden complete retraction can make it settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: Ground effect makes a low go-around feel better than it is, and climbing out of it too early can leave the airplane unable to climb.
cards.why: True. The performance is borrowed and repaid on leaving ground effect [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

cards.s: Once you accept a LAHSO clearance, a rejected landing is no longer allowed.
cards.why: False. A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing; keep separation and tell the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

cards.s: Wait for the controller to ask before reading back a LAHSO clearance, to keep the frequency clear.
cards.why: False. Controllers need a full readback of every LAHSO clearance, and pilots are encouraged to give it without prompting [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

cards.s: Settling onto the runway and bouncing during the start of a very low go-around is always dangerous and should be avoided by pulling up hard.
cards.why: False. It is not particularly dangerous if the airplane is kept straight at a constant, safe pitch; power soon gives flying speed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

activities.title: Landing lesson in a gusty crosswind
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your pre-solo learner is flying circuits with a gusty left crosswind within limits. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On base, the learner overshoots the extended centerline and starts adding left rudder to tighten the turn. What do you say?
steps.why: That is the setup for a skidding cross-control stall; the safest action for an overshoot is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: Next final: at 400 feet the learner is low and 6 knots slow. What is the first fix?
steps.why: Lower and slower is too little total energy: throttle up [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Raising the nose alone or raising flaps makes it worse [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: In the flare a gust hits and the learner balloons 15 feet, nose high, airspeed dropping fast. What now?
options: Push forward to get back down
Let them hold it and see
Go around now, before the stall; take the controls if they freeze
steps.why: When ballooning is excessive, go around immediately and apply power before a stall [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]. Take control without hesitation when needed [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: The learner freezes and pulls. You take over. What do you say?
steps.why: Take the controls and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls'; fighting a strong, anxious learner gains nothing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

steps.s: Two circuits later the learner lands with a slight drift and the upwind wing starts to rise on the rollout. What do you coach?
options: Aileron toward the high wing right away and keep direction
steps.why: Apply more aileron toward the high wing immediately; the sooner, the more effective [[24:208|AFH 9-37]].

activities.title: Teaching principles in the landing lesson
activities.intro: Tap a principle, then tap what it looks like when teaching landings.

pairs.r: Don't start landings on the first flight; build success first
Normal landings mastered before short-field and soft-field
An hour of only crosswind landings: looks good today, retained poorly
Deer cross the runway on final: stress being ready to go around
Brief, explicit feedback after each landing, no extra distractions
Fine on calm days, falls apart in a gusty crosswind
